title: The Spirit as Uncreated Revealer
english: They say that He, knowing only the things of God and being present over all, is such: 2.2 Moses in Genesis speaks from the face of God, saying, 'My spirit shall not remain in these men forever because they are flesh.' Haggai similarly speaks from a divine voice, 'I am with you, and my spirit has stood in your midst.' 2.3 Zechariah similarly says, 'But listen to my words, and receive my statutes, which I command by my spirit to my servants the prophets.' 2.4 Isaiah speaks of the Son from the Father, 'My spirit is upon you, and the words which I have given into your mouth shall not fail from your mouth and from the mouth of your seed'; he calls them 'seed', whom he also called to sonship. 2.5 And again from the Son, 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.' To complete these things in the economy, Matthew said thus, 'So that what was said through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, saying: "Behold my servant whom I have loved, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased; I will put my spirit upon him."' 2.6 And again from the Father, 'For a spirit shall proceed from me.' 2.7 And in Ezekiel, the Most High Father names our spirit 'your' spirit, but names the Holy Spirit his own, since it has proceeded from him according to nature: 'And I will give you a new heart and a new spirit; and I will take the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will give my spirit in you.' 2.8 And in Joel, 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh.' 2.9 And Paul wrote to Titus that these things have been accomplished: 'When the grace of our salvation appeared, not according to works which we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy, having regenerated us through the bath of rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out upon us richly through Jesus Christ.' 2.10 And when did he pour out? When Christ, breathing, was saying, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' And also the 'poured out', since water from him proceeds similarly and divine myrrh, which will be shown to us in the fitting places at the right time. 2.11 And the 'upon all flesh.' For these words fit the shared essence of the Holy Trinity, not the unshared created rational nature; for not...

What is written does not say, 'I will pour out from the archangel,' but 'from my spirit,' and not in such a broad manner, but 'upon all flesh.' David, entreating, cries, 'Do not take your holy spirit from me' (Psalm 51:11), and again, 'Your holy spirit shall guide me in a straight path' (Psalm 139:24). Matthew says from the Son, 'It is not you who speak, but the spirit of my Father speaking in you' (Matthew 10:20), which is to say: not you the creatures, but the uncreated spirit of God.

Paul also writes to the Corinthians in the first epistle, 'What eye has not seen, and what ear has not heard, and what has not come up upon the heart of man: what God has prepared for those who love him, which God has revealed to us through his spirit. The spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For what does a man know of the things of the man, if not the spirit of the man that is in him? In the same way, no one knows the things of God, if not the spirit of God. But we have not received a spirit of the world, but the spirit which is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God' (1 Corinthians 2:9-12).

The 'prepared' good things from God, he said, that 'the spirit' 'revealed' as a companion; and 'his spirit' by antithesis to our own spirit. And securing again that it not be thought of as an angel or some other created spirit, he brought forward: 'we have not received a spirit of the world'—that is, a generated one—'but the spirit which is from God'—that is, from the remaining [essence], the one proceeding from the subsistence of God; and as it alone knows the things of God, as Lord, and having likewise toward the Father according to nature. For the 'servant,' as it says in the Gospel, 'does not know what his lord does' (Luke 12:30).

No longer, however, did he speak as if regarding the man who dwells 'in God,' so that the uncomposed God might be thought of as composite. To the Ephesians: 'Do not grieve the holy spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption' (Ephesians 4:30); to the Romans: 'you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if the spirit of God dwells in you; but if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he is not his' (Romans 8:9); to the Galatians: 'because you are sons, God has sent the spirit of his son into your hearts, crying Abba Father' (Galatians 4:6); to the Philippians: 'for I know that...'

title: The Spirit as Uncreated God
english: This will result to me for salvation, through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Therefore, look, just as the saying 'Spirit of God' alone, and the addition of 'of' and 'your', has clearly signified this, that it is also uncreated and is God, having a name that is not acquired, but from being that which is naturally what is also attributed to it.

And the fact that it is written 'Spirit of the Son' similarly demonstrated the communion of nature toward him, so that it might not be considered a creature of his. For how could the Son have created that which is and has also been written 'Spirit of God' to his own Father, as if he did not have it from himself before this? Which is not only blasphemous, but also a lie. 'Spirit of Christ' might be understood, that is, the power of Christ, in the manner that it has been said, 'the power of Christ and the wisdom of God.' For since the blessed Hypostases themselves proceeded from the nature of one Father and not by a creative energy, they lead back to the same one.

In order that no one might suspect his being a beginning or an end, but might truly believe that it is the Spirit of God, proceeding according to his nature, breathed uncaused and not becoming, as one of the other functional spirits, the Lord teaches in the Gospel according to John, saying: 'the Spirit of truth, which proceeds from the Father' (John 15:26). And he did not say 'is created.' For every birth and procession is accomplished through equal and similar things; but most distinctly is the birth and procession from the one Father through the union of his own divinity.

But regarding creatures, the prototype leads in time; but regarding God, it is not so, but co-essential and co-proceeded. And agreeing with the Lord, John proclaimed the Holy Spirit, which is equal and unalterable to the Father, and as a partial grace of him, encompassing, as one might say, the undefinable God the Father, and showing it as a partial grace found among the faithful, saying: 'For by this we know that we abide in him, and he in us, by the Spirit he has given us' (1 John 4:13). In the manner that the Son said: 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:7/14:9); and: 'I proceeded from the Father' (John 16:28). For nothing at all according to essence...

title: The Divine Names of the Holy Spirit
english: That calling him the true Son and the true Spirit denotes the appropriation of nature by God: but regarding all other things, it differs by lordship or by faith; just as we are accustomed to say regarding those who are of the same substance to us, 'my son, my spirit,' but regarding others, 'my field, my horse,' yet also 'my God.'

For the manner of the hypostatic Logos of the divine nature is not shown to have become Son and only-begotten and the Word of God, Christ, by simply and unattachedly speaking, but by having the syllable of 'my' and 'your' joined together. As when God says, 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17), and again, 'my good Word,' and, 'I prepared a lamp for my Christ'; and we say, 'your Son, your only-begotten, your Christ.'

Nor does it being called by the same name or by a similar name regarding us—'sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?' (Ps 38:13)—bring forth the Son of God through the homonymy of divinity; likewise, the Holy Spirit does not simply being called 'Spirit,' but the joining to the name, or as being from God the 'my,' or as being from the creation the 'your,' or even the word 'holy' or 'incorruptible' or 'eternal,' denotes that he proceeds from the Father's hypostasis; nor does the speaking of the liturgical things and our spirits or holy or eternal things by the same name bring forth that he is by nature the true Spirit of God.

For in the riddles concerning him, some declaration of his divine nature and power is always found. But the creatures received the holy and eternal toward their own nature, not possessing these things by nature from themselves.

Since even these heretics are found arguing against themselves, that the 'my' regarding the Son of God and the 'holy' and the 'eternal' they simply accept as announcing the identity of the divine nature? Furthermore, in these matters, he did not name our soul 'spirit' in the proofs provided, but his own Holy Spirit. For having our own spirit, the Spirit of God was given to us. For the Father said, 'My Spirit shall not remain in these men' (cf. Ps 105:36), and the Son: 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22). It is clear.

And, as it was said concerning the divine Spirit, that it is like our own indwelling Spirit. Therefore, just as the Son, the Word of God, is paternally generative, so the Holy Spirit is spiritually proceeding and not by creation. And just as there is no change in essence, power, or glory for the only-begotten Son in relation to God the Father—though any difference, if it is permissible to say so, exists in relation to creation—so also with the one divine Spirit.

Thus, it is more righteous not even to hear the heretics and to approach listening to these things. Concerning how the divine nature of the Holy Spirit is signified by various names. What we have said from the beginning, the words testify a second time: that there are various God-befitting names for the Spirit of God, having laid upon them much other emphasis and a relation surpassing all, contributing to the present theorems continuously and more excellently than the most appropriate interpretation, to both the Father and the Son.

And still replenishing both his divine nature and his authentic power, and comforting our weakness regarding our ability to reach him either by the interpretation of words or by the contemplation of the mind, and providing boldness to call him without danger consubstantial with God and to believe in his sanctification. And we find nothing of the other spirits privileged to be called by these names; but these things, which alone exist by nature, are not one of the many things, but God.

And these names are these: Holy Spirit, as it is written everywhere; Spirit of holiness, and Sanctifier, as he writes to the Romans: 'Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and was designated the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness' (Rom 1:1-4). And again: 'that the offering of the Gentiles might be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit' (Rom 15:16), and likewise: 'we must always thank God for all of you, beloved brothers, because God chose you as a firstfruit for salvation in the sanctification of the Spirit and in the faith of truth' (1 Thess 2:13).
